passage: My cousin Anand used to point and shout "ba-ba-da!" at everything. When I visited this month, he tugged my dupatta toward the fridge and said, "Milk." Later he held up his empty cup: "More milk!" His mother laughed. At bath time he said, "No bath," and ran behind the curtain. I'm Deepika, and I don't know exactly what goes on in his head, but his words got him what he wanted far quicker than pointing ever did.

qa.q: What did Anand say when he held up his empty cup?
qa.a: He said, "More milk!"

qa.q: How did Anand seem to feel about bath time when he said "No bath" and hid?
qa.a: He seemed reluctant and cross about the bath, so he said "No bath" and hid behind the curtain to avoid it.

qa.q: How could Anand's family encourage more words?
qa.a: They can answer his words quickly, repeat them back a little longer, like "More milk, please", and give him time to talk.

qa.q: How does Deepika see the change in Anand?
qa.a: She notices his words work better than pointing did, but admits she can't be sure what he is thinking.

grounding: Shows a toddler moving from babble to single words and short phrases that get his needs met.

passage: First week: Jomon, eighteen months, points at the banana bunch and says, "Ba! Ba!" Tarun, his father, offers a biscuit; Jomon wails and points harder. Tarun asks, "Banana?" and Jomon goes quiet. Two weeks later, Jomon says, "Nana," and Tarun hands one over. A month on, at breakfast, Jomon pushes his plate away. "Nana, Appa. Want nana."

qa.q: What did Tarun first offer instead of a banana?
qa.a: A biscuit.

qa.q: Why did Jomon wail when he got the biscuit?
qa.a: He was frustrated because he wanted the banana and his sound wasn't understood.

qa.q: What helped Jomon move from "Ba" to a real word?
qa.a: Tarun naming the fruit, "Banana?", gave him a clear word to copy.

qa.q: How is breakfast different for Tarun a month later?
qa.a: He no longer has to guess; Jomon tells him in a short sentence what he wants.

grounding: Shows a toddler progressing over weeks from a babbled sound to a word and a short sentence to ask for food.

passage: At the crowded vegetable market in Chennai, Shankar, two, rides on his mother Chandrika's hip. He spots a man selling balloons. "Ball-oon! Amma, ball-oon!" She keeps walking. He pats her cheek. "Amma. Red one. Please." Chandrika stops, surprised; he has never said please before. She buys one red balloon and holds the string for him. "Mine," he says, reaching up high.

qa.q: What colour of balloon did Shankar ask for?
qa.a: A red one.

qa.q: Why was Chandrika surprised?
qa.a: Shankar had never said please before, so the new word caught her off guard.

qa.q: What could Chandrika do to keep Shankar using new words?
qa.a: She can reply when he talks in short phrases and name things around them in the market.

qa.q: What would change if Shankar could only point and cry?
qa.a: Chandrika might not know what he wanted in the busy market, and both could end up frustrated.

grounding: Shows a toddler using a short sentence to ask for what he wants in a busy city market.

passage:
"Siddharth, what do you want?"
"Mmm-ba!"
Pankaj, the boy's father, points. "Ball?"
"Ba!"
"Say ball."
"Bah!" Siddharth, eighteen months, stretches his arms toward the shelf.
Pankaj brings it down. "Here's the ball."
Siddharth hugs it. "More ba!" he says, pointing at a second ball.
"More ball? You said more!"
Siddharth grins and bounces.

qa.q: What did Siddharth point at when he said "More ba"?
qa.a: He pointed at a second ball.

qa.q: What does Siddharth's bouncing and grinning suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he is happy and proud that his father understood him.

qa.q: How does Pankaj help Siddharth's speech?
qa.a: He repeats the correct word, 'ball', and praises Siddharth when he joins words.

qa.q: What would change if Pankaj ignored Siddharth's early sounds?
qa.a: Siddharth might feel less encouraged to keep trying to use words to ask for things.

grounding: Shows a toddler moving from babbling toward functional words and a two-word phrase to ask for things.

passage:
Daycare note, Sumit (teacher), Friday.

Amandeep, two, used a short sentence today: "Me want water." Until last month she mostly pointed and said "uh-uh." This week she's also said "Mama gone" and "No sleep." When I didn't understand "ba-na," she pulled me to the fruit basket. I repeated "banana" and she said "nana!" I'll keep narrating our routines and give her time to answer. 👍

qa.q: What short sentence did Amandeep use today?
qa.a: She said, "Me want water."

qa.q: Why did Amandeep pull Sumit to the fruit basket?
qa.a: She wanted Sumit to understand her and was determined to get the banana.

qa.q: How is Sumit supporting Amandeep's speech?
qa.a: By repeating words clearly, narrating routines and giving her time to answer.

qa.q: How might Amandeep's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They'd likely be pleased to hear her moving from pointing to short sentences.

grounding: Shows a teacher noting a toddler moving from pointing and babbling to short sentences about her needs.

passage: "Ba-ba-ba," Hansa used to shout at the goats. This week, standing in the courtyard with Nirmala, her Dadi, she pointed at the black kid goat and said, "Bakri." Then, when it nosed her hand: "Bakri, no!" Nirmala stopped sweeping. At the hand pump Hansa held out her tin cup and said, "Paani, Dadi, more." Nirmala filled it to the top and repeated each word back to her, slowly.

qa.q: What did Hansa call the black kid goat?
qa.a: She called it "Bakri."

qa.q: What might Nirmala have felt when she stopped sweeping?
qa.a: She was probably surprised and delighted to hear Hansa's first real words and a tiny sentence.

qa.q: How could Nirmala keep encouraging Hansa's talking?
qa.a: Keep repeating Hansa's words back clearly and adding one more word, so Hansa hears slightly longer phrases.

qa.q: What would change for Hansa if nobody answered her new words?
qa.a: She would get less reward for trying and might go back to pointing and shouting instead of talking.

grounding: Shows a toddler in a village moving from babbling to single words and short phrases to ask for what she needs.

passage: Kaito had spent months saying "da" for everything in the Madrid flat. On Tuesday he stood at the fridge, slapped the door, and said, "Milk." Lucia, his mother, froze with the kettle in her hand. "Milk? You want milk?" "Milk. Cup. Blue cup." She poured it into the blue cup. Kaito drank, set it down, and said, "More," very firmly, as if he had always been able to.

qa.q: What did Kaito ask for at the fridge?
qa.a: Milk, in the blue cup.

qa.q: Why did Lucia freeze with the kettle in her hand?
qa.a: She was surprised and thrilled to hear Kaito use real words after months of only saying "da". 😊

qa.q: How could Lucia build on this moment?
qa.a: Give him what he asks for when he uses words and repeat them back in short phrases, like "milk in the blue cup".

qa.q: What is it like for Kaito when his words finally get him what he wants?
qa.a: It likely feels powerful and satisfying, which is why he said "More" so firmly.

grounding: Shows a toddler moving from a single babbled sound to words and short phrases that get his needs met.

passage: I'm Raghav, and on Holi morning I was in charge of my little brother Kunal while our parents greeted the neighbours. Last Holi he just babbled and screamed at the colours. This time he held up his wet hands and said, "Pink! Kunal pink!" When a water balloon burst near him, he shouted, "Bhaiya, again!" I can't tell what he meant by everything, but he talked all morning.

qa.q: What did Kunal shout when the water balloon burst?
qa.a: He shouted, "Bhaiya, again!"

qa.q: What does Kunal's "Bhaiya, again!" suggest he felt?
qa.a: He seemed excited and happy, wanting more of the fun instead of being scared by the burst.

qa.q: How could Raghav help Kunal keep using new words during the festival?
qa.a: Name the colours and actions back to him and wait for him to try, rather than answering for him.

qa.q: How does Raghav see the change in Kunal since last Holi?
qa.a: Raghav notices Kunal moving from babbling and screaming to short phrases, even if not every word is clear.

grounding: Shows a toddler's talk growing from babble to short phrases, seen by an older brother during a festival.

passage:
First day of the wedding week. Damini, twenty months, points at the laddoo tray and shouts, "Aaa!" Farhan, her papa, says, "Laddoo? Say laddoo." She just points harder.
Mehendi night. In the crowd, Damini tugs Farhan's kurta and says, "Du. Du!" He hands her one, laughing.
The morning after the wedding. At breakfast she says clearly, "Papa, more laddoo," and every aunty at the table cheers.

qa.q: What does Damini say at breakfast after the wedding?
qa.a: Papa, more laddoo.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when she pointed harder at the tray?
qa.a: Damini felt frustrated and impatient, wanting the laddoo but not yet able to say it.

qa.q: How did Farhan help Damini find her words?
qa.a: He named the laddoo and invited her to say it, then answered her attempt 'du' by handing one over.

qa.q: How might the aunties feel when they cheer?
qa.a: The aunties feel delighted and amused, celebrating her new sentence along with the wedding.

grounding: Across a winter wedding week, a toddler moves from pointing and sounds to a short sentence.

passage: During Ganesh Chaturthi, the drums from the pandal shook the windows of their Pune flat. Vishal, two, stood on the sofa, pointing. "Dum dum!" His mother, Disha, picked him up. "Drums. Big drums. Shall we see Ganpati?" "Ganpati see!" They went down to the lane as the idol passed. Vishal waved both hands and shouted, "Bappa! Bye Bappa!" A man nearby laughed and shouted back, "Morya!"

qa.q: What did Vishal call the drums at first?
qa.a: Dum dum.

qa.q: How did Vishal feel as the idol passed?
qa.a: Vishal was excited and joyful, waving both hands and shouting.

qa.q: How did Disha help Vishal's language grow?
qa.a: She repeated his word as the proper one, 'Drums. Big drums', and asked a simple question he could answer.

qa.q: How might the man nearby feel hearing Vishal shout?
qa.a: The man seemed amused and warm, joining in with 'Morya!'

grounding: During Ganesh Chaturthi in Pune, a toddler moves from sound words to short phrases with his mother's help.

passage:
"Mehak, what do you want?" Sarika asked at the kulfi cart. The May heat made everything sticky.
Mehak, two, pointed. "Dat."
"Which one? Mango or pista?"
"Mango."
"Mango kulfi. Say please."
"Pees."
"Good. Here you go."
Mehak licked it and frowned. "Cold!"
"Yes, very cold."
"Mehak cold!" She held out her sticky hand.
"You want me to hold it?"
"Mamma hold." Mehak shook her fingers, then grabbed the kulfi back. "Mehak eat!"

qa.q: Which kulfi did Mehak choose?
qa.a: Mango.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling when she said 'Cold!' and frowned?
qa.a: Mehak was surprised and a little uncomfortable at how cold the kulfi was.

qa.q: How did Sarika help Mehak use more words?
qa.a: She offered a choice between two flavours, modelled 'please', and repeated Mehak's words back.

qa.q: How might Sarika feel when Mehak grabs the kulfi back?
qa.a: Sarika probably found it funny and sweet, seeing her daughter's growing will and words.

grounding: On a hot May evening, a toddler uses new words and two-word phrases to choose and manage a kulfi.

passage:
Daycare note, rainy season.

Pallavi, twenty months, used to say only "ba" for everything. This week, watching the rain from the window, she said "rain!" and then "more rain!" when it got heavier.

At snack time she held up her empty cup: "Milk gone." Twice.

I'm naming everything we see outside and waiting for her to try. Told her mother at pickup; she was thrilled 😊 — Zeenat

qa.q: What did Pallavi say when the rain got heavier?
qa.a: She said "more rain!"

qa.q: How did Pallavi's mother feel on hearing the news?
qa.a: Her mother was thrilled and happy about Pallavi's new words.

qa.q: What is Zeenat doing to support Pallavi's speech, and why does it help?
qa.a: She names everything they see and waits for Pallavi to try, giving her words to copy and time to speak.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel when she says "milk gone" and gets more?
qa.a: Pallavi might feel pleased and understood, which encourages her to use more words.

grounding: A daycare note records a toddler moving from babbling to short two-word phrases about rain and snack time.

passage:
Christmas week in the village near Champhai meant stars on every roof. Lalremsiami, not yet two, stood on the veranda with her cousin Seema.

"Star," Seema said, pointing.

"Tar," Lalremsiami said.

When the church bell rang, she pointed and said, "Bell!" Then she tugged Seema's hand toward the kitchen. "Cake. More cake."

Seema laughed and took her in.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami say when the church bell rang?
qa.a: She pointed and said, "Bell!"

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami want when she tugged Seema's hand?
qa.a: She was eager and excited for more cake, using words to show what she wanted.

qa.q: How did Seema help Lalremsiami's words grow?
qa.a: She named things like the star and responded when Lalremsiami asked for cake, showing that words get results.

qa.q: How might Seema feel hearing Lalremsiami ask for "more cake"?
qa.a: Seema was amused and pleased, laughing as she took her to the kitchen.

grounding: During Christmas in a Mizoram village, a toddler moves from single words to a short phrase to ask for what she wants.

passage:
During Tet, the apartment in Hanoi was full of peach blossoms and aunties. Bao, two, clung to Valentina, the babysitter, who had come to help.

An auntie held out a red envelope. Bao stared.

"Say thank you," Valentina whispered.

Bao said, "Cam!" and grabbed it.

Later, when his cousin took his toy car, he shouted, "Mine car! Bao car!"

Valentina blinked. That was his first three-word sentence she had heard.

qa.q: What did Bao shout when his cousin took his toy car?
qa.a: He shouted, "Mine car! Bao car!"

qa.q: How was Bao feeling when he shouted about the toy car?
qa.a: Bao was upset and angry that his cousin took it, and used words to say so.

qa.q: How could Valentina support Bao's new speech?
qa.a: She could repeat his words back in a full sentence, like "Yes, that's Bao's car," and help him ask for it back.

qa.q: What was it like for Valentina to hear Bao's new words?
qa.a: Valentina was surprised and probably pleased, since it was the first time she heard him put so many words together.

grounding: During Tet, a toddler starts using short sentences to communicate what he wants.

passage: I'm Rajni, and I sell vegetables at the gate of Sabina's building. For months Sabina just babbled at me, "ba-ba-da", and pointed. This morning she tugged her Ammi's dupatta, looked at my basket and said, "Mango. Want mango." Her cousin Farhan, holding her other hand, shouted, "Two words!" and asked her to say it again. She did, louder, and held out both hands. I can't know what went on in that little head, but she wasn't pointing anymore.

qa.q: What did Sabina say when she looked at the basket?
qa.a: She said, "Mango. Want mango."

qa.q: What does Sabina holding out both hands suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt eager and pleased, confident that her words would get her the mango.

qa.q: How could Sabina's family encourage her new words?
qa.a: They could answer her words quickly and repeat them back a little longer, like "You want a mango? Here's a mango."

qa.q: How does Farhan react to Sabina's new words?
qa.a: Farhan is thrilled and wants to hear it again, as if the two words are a big event for the whole family.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler moving from babbling and pointing to a short sentence that asks for what she wants.
